questions.enonce_markdown: a) Why was Esau rejected as one of the patriarchs in Israel? [10 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
Esau, the elder twin of Isaac and Rebekah, was not chosen to carry the covenant line, and the Genesis account gives several reasons.

1. **He despised his birthright.** In Genesis 25 Esau, tired and hungry, sold his birthright to Jacob for a meal of lentil stew, and the narrator says that he despised it. The birthright carried leadership of the family, a larger share of the inheritance and a religious role, so selling it showed that he did not value the covenant.
2. **He lacked self-control and spiritual concern.** He acted on the appetite of the moment, which is a mark of a man unfit to guard the promise.
3. **His marriages grieved his parents.** Genesis 26 reports that he married Hittite women, who made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah. The patriarchs avoided marrying the local peoples in order to protect their faith.
4. **God's prior choice.** Before the twins were born Rebekah received an oracle that the elder would serve the younger (Genesis 25). The narrative presents the covenant line as following God's choice and not the custom of the firstborn.
5. **The blessing passed to Jacob.** In Genesis 27 Isaac blessed Jacob, and the blessing could not be recalled. Esau became the ancestor of Edom, a separate people.

**Conclusion.** Esau was rejected because of his own attitude, his marriages and above all the free choice of God.

questions.enonce_markdown: b) What factors prove that Jacob was chosen by God? [15 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Jacob, the younger son of Isaac, became the third patriarch and was renamed Israel. The book of Genesis gives several signs that his place was the result of God's choice and not only of his own scheming.

**1. The oracle before birth.** Rebekah was told that two nations were in her womb and that the elder would serve the younger (Genesis 25). Jacob was marked out by God before he could do anything.

**2. The birthright and the blessing.** Jacob obtained the birthright from Esau (Genesis 25) and the blessing of Isaac (Genesis 27). The narrative holds that the blessing could not be taken back, which shows that the outcome was accepted as the will of God in spite of the deception.

**3. The vision at Bethel.** While fleeing from Esau, Jacob dreamed of a stairway between earth and heaven (Genesis 28). God stood above it and renewed to him the promises made to Abraham and Isaac: land, many descendants and a blessing for all families of the earth. God also promised to be with him and to bring him back.

**4. God's protection and prosperity in exile.** Jacob served Laban for many years, married Leah and Rachel and returned with large flocks and a family (Genesis 29 to 31). The text attributes his survival and growth to the presence of God.

**5. The struggle at the Jabbok and the new name.** At Peniel (Genesis 32) Jacob wrestled with a divine figure and was given the name Israel. The name later became that of the whole nation, a mark of divine approval.

**6. The reconciliation with Esau and the renewal at Bethel.** Esau, who had threatened him, received him peacefully (Genesis 33), and at Bethel God confirmed the name Israel and the promises (Genesis 35).

**7. The twelve sons.** His sons became the ancestors of the twelve tribes, and through Joseph the family was preserved in Egypt.

**Conclusion.** The oracle, the vision at Bethel, God's protection, the new name and the founding of the twelve tribes all show, according to Genesis, that Jacob was chosen by God and not merely successful by his own efforts.
